title: Interview with Jerry Crisci: AI Is Changing the World. Who's Redesigning School? September 8, 2026
author: Stefan Bauschard
source: AI x Higher Ed Podcast, Stefan Bauschard's Substack (stefanbauschard.substack.com),
summary: In this AI x Higher Ed Podcast interview, Jerry Crisci, former director of Scarsdale's Center for Innovation, argues that school innovation ultimately reduces to one word, permission, and that AI represents a uniquely disruptive exigency because it combines unprecedented adoption speed, radically divergent public 'lenses' on its meaning, and unclear ownership of learning compared to prior technologies. He describes developing the FAIR framework (Futuring, AI, Innovation, Redesign) after observing that schools were redesigning instruction only for AI as it currently exists rather than confronting what school itself might need to become, and explains he deliberately opens with AI content first specifically because it manufactures the urgency needed before futuring and redesign work can proceed. Crisci pushes back on device-ban legislation like New York's proposed FOCUS Act, using Scarsdale's technology-dependent fifth-grade research project to argue blanket bans conflict with basic instructional needs, and instead endorses the University of Chicago's tripartite framing of teaching with, about, and without AI. His signature classroom technique demystifies AI by showing students, via a live simulator, that a language model builds text word by word through pattern matching rather than thought, a distinction he argues is essential given reports of students forming AI relationships they mistake for real ones. He closes by calling for national-level urgency, comparable to Cold War-era investment, including dedicated lab schools and research institutions focused specifically on AI's five-year workforce implications for education.
points: Reduces the abstract concept of 'school innovation' to a single operational test - do people in the organization actually have permission to experiment - rather than treating it as a matter of resources or willpower alone.

Identifies three specific properties (speed/acceleration, divergent public 'lenses,' and unclear ownership of learning) that distinguish AI's disruption from every prior educational technology adoption, giving a concrete framework for why AI feels different rather than just asserting that it is.

Reveals the deliberately engineered sequencing behind his FAIR framework: AI content is presented first specifically to manufacture urgency, since presenting the redesign work without that urgency produced schools redesigning instruction around current AI rather than reimagining school itself.

Uses a concrete counter-example (Scarsdale's technology-dependent fifth-grade capstone research project) to push back on blanket device-ban legislation like New York's FOCUS Act, showing where such policy collides with existing, valued instructional practice.

Demonstrates a specific, transferable classroom technique for AI literacy: live-simulating how a language model constructs a sentence word by word through pattern matching, explicitly framed as a defense against students mistaking AI interaction for a relationship with a person.
quotes: If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative

If you're going to be running any kind of innovation in your organization, the bottom line is: do people in your organization have the permission to experiment and do things that would be truly innovative? Our superintendent wisely said, when we founded our center, that technology was the fulcrum, not the focus.

The difference with AI, I would say, is that it has three components that the rest of technology didn't have: speed, or acceleration, we've never seen a technology be this quickly adopted and this fast-moving; lenses, people looking at this technology through all different lenses, with AI everyone has different viewpoints; and ownership, with technology it was pretty clear who owned the learning, teachers were in control of things, with AI we don't have ownership clearly defined.

I realized that teachers were doing a great job of redesigning their curriculum and instruction with schools as they currently are and with AI as they currently were, and I said this is not going to continue down this path, I really need to make people more aware of what the future of school could be.

There's a bill in New York, the FOCUS Act, that wants to ban all internet-connected devices in grades kindergarten through fifth grade. We had all of our fifth graders in Scarsdale do an independent research project, and they had to do internet research. What do you do if they have no technology?

I use an AI simulator. I show them how it constructs a sentence word by word. I also show them that it's not really thinking. It's pattern matching. I think that is so important, not just for teachers to understand, but when you hear about students engaging in relationships with AI, thinking of that as a person. Here's what's happening behind the scenes, it simulates that you're talking to a person, but in fact you're talking to a broken calculator.
There should be a national initiative that really creates almost a series of lab schools and a dedicated research institution to focus on AI and education.
